solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: North Sea's rejected French produce

indicators.note: something rejected is turned away, so the compass point is thrown out of the sea word

parts.note: the briny is a jocular name for the sea, and brine is salt water
N is the compass abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Fishermen complain that their North Sea catch has been turned away by French buyers.
explanation.walkthrough: Read it as 'North, sea's rejected': BRINE loses its N to leave BRIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Brie is a soft cheese made in the region of that name east of Paris, so it is a French product.

clue.text: Form erected in circle of unobtrusive aspect

indicators.note: one word sits inside the other, as the clue says it is placed within
in a down clue something erected is stood upright, so the word reads from the bottom up

parts.note: a rite is a set ceremonial form

explanation.surface: Sounds like a sculpture stood up inside a ring that keeps a low profile.
explanation.definitionFit: A retiring person is shy and avoids attention, so modest and unobtrusive in manner.

clue.text: I start to see Loch and Lewis and Harris, possibly

indicators.note: the start of the following word is all that is wanted from it

parts.note: L is the map abbreviation for a loch or lake

explanation.surface: A tourist describes beginning to take in the lochs of the Western Isles.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis and Harris look like two places but are the two parts of a single Hebridean landmass, hence 'possibly' for an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis and Harris is one island in the Outer Hebrides, so it is an example of the general term.

clue.text: Very small chap, after brief time, used social media?

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
a man's name standing for any chap

explanation.surface: A tiny man who, after a moment, posted something online.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' tells you the chap comes after the time, with the small word between.
explanation.definitionFit: To tweet is to post a short message on Twitter, the best-known social media platform.

clue.text: Elk tries hobbling (it only has three legs)

indicators.note: a hobbling creature walks awkwardly and out of step, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: An elk trying to walk badly, explained by its missing a leg.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket is the definition, joked onto the limping elk; the Isle of Man flag shows the classic example.
explanation.definitionFit: A triskele is a symbol of three bent legs or spirals radiating from a centre, as on the Manx flag.

clue.text: One old King brought in to observe rising tidal waters

indicators.note: these letters are carried inside the verb that follows
in a down entry rising means reading from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Georgius Rex, the royal cipher of King George

explanation.surface: A former monarch is taken to watch the tide come in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' turns only the verb upwards; the one and the king sit inside it. Eagre is a dialect word mostly met on the Trent and Humber.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagre is a tidal bore, a wave that surges up a river such as the Trent on a high tide.

clue.text: Power delivered from upsurge in new free gas

indicators.note: an upward surge in a down clue makes everything read bottom to top
something delivered from a place is released out of it, so that letter goes

parts.note: open, as in free to all
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: Sounds like an energy story about a surge in a new kind of free gas supply.
explanation.walkthrough: N and OPEN join, P is removed to leave NOEN, and that whole string is turned upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Neon is a noble gas, an inert element used in glowing advertising signs.

clue.text: Fire raging in Grammar School — sad events

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are placed within the school abbreviation
a raging fire is wild and out of control, so its letters run riot

explanation.surface: A blaze sweeping through a grammar school, a run of terrible incidents.
explanation.walkthrough: A grammar school is a selective British state secondary school.
explanation.definitionFit: Griefs used as a countable plural means sorrows, the occasions or causes of deep distress.

clue.text: Items for sale, including magazine backing military exercises

indicators.note: the sale items take the other word inside them

parts.note: wares are goods offered for sale

indicators.note: going backwards, so the magazine word reads right to left

explanation.surface: Merchandise and a magazine that supports army manoeuvres.
explanation.definitionFit: War games are simulated battles or manoeuvres staged for training, that is, exercises by armed forces.

clue.text: NT's domain badly affected by time — Queen's intervening

indicators.note: to intervene is to come between, so the royal letters go inside

parts.note: an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: The National Trust's estates are suffering with the years, with royalty getting involved.
explanation.walkthrough: The NT is the National Trust, the British charity that looks after historic houses and landscapes.
explanation.definitionFit: The National Trust's remit is preserving historic buildings and landscape, the nation's inherited legacy.

clue.text: Doing Dad's job is ultimately exhausting, though not at first

indicators.note: the opening letter is not there
ultimately points to the final letter of the word before

explanation.surface: A weary parent remarks that fatherhood wears you out in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' looks like it qualifies 'exhausting' but picks the last letter of 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Siring offspring is fathering them, the biological part a father plays.

clue.text: Leader of professors kept in university loop, in position to avoid stink

indicators.note: something kept in is held inside the following letters

parts.note: to wind is to coil or loop

indicators.note: the leader is the first in line, so only the initial is used

explanation.surface: A senior academic held in a campus circuit, placed to escape a bad smell.
explanation.walkthrough: The P goes between U and WIND, which together are the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing on the side the breeze comes from keeps a smell carried away from you.

clue.text: Extremely formal article in pole position

explanation.surface: A stiffly correct item sitting at the front of the grid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' is part of the definition of prim, not a signal for the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Prima is the Italian feminine for first, as in prima donna, so leading like a racer at the front.

clue.text: Anglican service still scheduled after Sunday? Good

indicators.note: after sends the scheduled word to follow the day abbreviation instead of preceding it

explanation.surface: Asking whether a church service is still going ahead after Sunday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' means even, as in 'even more'; ON comes after S in the answer although the clue lists them the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: Evensong is evening prayer in the Church of England, sung at the end of the day.

clue.text: Run from lover upset by new book such as Brave New World

definitions.text: book such as Brave New World

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disturbed, so these letters fall out of order
taken from means removed out of the following word

explanation.surface: Fleeing an upset partner, by way of a dystopian book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' places N beside the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Aldous Huxley's Brave New World is a work of long prose fiction, the defining kind of book.

clue.text: Success with channel involving new fixing device

indicators.note: the channel takes in the letter, involving it in its middle

parts.note: a gut is a narrow channel or strait

explanation.surface: A triumph for a TV station with a newly launched gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel' looks like television; a gut is a narrow water channel.
explanation.definitionFit: A wing nut has two flat lugs for turning by hand and fastens onto a bolt.

clue.text: Article seized by officer swamped by excessive wave

indicators.note: something seized is held fast inside what grabs it
swamped means engulfed, so this goes wholly inside the next word

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece grabbed by an officer who is overwhelmed by too great a wave.
explanation.definitionFit: To undulate is to move with a rising and falling motion, like a wave.

clue.text: Talk angrily after Department becomes corrupt

parts.note: to rave is to rant wildly

explanation.surface: An office ranting after its staff go bad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the department first.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to make someone morally bad or degraded.

clue.text: Tenor Verdi role Spanish composer's taken around Spain

indicators.note: the composer's name is placed around the country letter

parts.note: Joaquín Rodrigo, composer of the Concierto de Aranjuez
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: A Spanish composer has taken a Verdi tenor part around his homeland.
explanation.definitionFit: Roderigo is the Venetian gentleman in Verdi's Otello, a part written for a tenor singer.

clue.text: Idly — see — shifting covers for lights?

indicators.note: shifting means moving about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A lazy instruction to look at moving lampshades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lights' is old slang for eyes, as in 'punch his lights out'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lights is slang for eyes, and the lids are the folds of skin that close over them.

clue.text: Nasty baddy encompassing end of Kennedy for sure, with consistent impact

indicators.note: a nasty twist leaves the letters in an ugly new order
the end of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A wicked villain targeting a Kennedy with steady, certain effect.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens day by day comes regularly and steadily, gradually having its effect.

clue.text: Term for singing adopted by newly-wed British composer

indicators.note: something adopted is taken into the family, so it goes inside
a term is an end point, so only the last letter of the next word counts

explanation.surface: A recently married British composer takes up a word for vocal music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Term' looks like a word for a word; here it means the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Bridge was an English composer and violist, best remembered as Benjamin Britten's teacher.

clue.text: Absurdly simple thing to draw, duplicating a different character

indicators.note: a different letter is the one doubled, replacing the original pair's second member

parts.note: to doodle is to draw aimlessly

explanation.surface: Something so easy to sketch you only have to repeat a different letter.
explanation.walkthrough: DOODLE doubles the O; doubling the D instead gives the answer. A doddle is British slang for a very easy task.
explanation.definitionFit: A doddle is British informal for a task so easy it is laughable, a piece of cake.

clue.text: Located near churchman, daughter turned up in a church

indicators.note: in a down entry turned up means read upwards

explanation.surface: A girl turns up at church and is seated close to the clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the words after 'daughter' are turned up. Decani is Latin for 'of the dean'.
explanation.definitionFit: Decani marks the dean's side of a cathedral choir, the south side, so near that cleric.

clue.text: Mercenary imprisons one offering excuse

indicators.note: to imprison is to lock inside, so one letter is put within

explanation.surface: A hired soldier locks up a man who is making excuses.
explanation.definitionFit: A venial sin or fault is a minor one that can be pardoned, so it allows an excuse.

clue.text: European to ponder tailless and flightless birds

indicators.note: without its tail, the last letter is lost

explanation.surface: A continental thinker contemplates birds lacking both tails and flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailless' seems to describe the birds but belongs to the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Emus are large Australian ratites that cannot fly.

clue.text: E Coli spread, enveloping most of pudding and sweet in America

indicators.note: to envelop is to wrap around, so the letters surround the pudding
bacteria that spread scatter about, so the letters get scattered too
most but not all, so the last letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A food-poisoning outbreak contaminating desserts and sweets in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: The British spelling is liquorice; American English writes it with a C.
explanation.definitionFit: Licorice is the American spelling of the black chewy confection flavoured with root extract.

clue.text: She ruled company, putting squeeze on the French

indicators.note: squeezing something holds it tight inside

explanation.surface: A female boss whose firm leans on the French.
explanation.walkthrough: Cleo is the short form of Cleopatra, queen of Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleopatra, familiarly Cleo, reigned over Ptolemaic Egypt, a female monarch.

clue.text: See occupying Cornish resort beginning to disappoint: assessed resources

indicators.note: the verb occupies, sitting within the resort

parts.note: Bude is a seaside town in north Cornwall
to get it is to see, understand

indicators.note: only the start of the next word is used

explanation.surface: Visitors to a Cornish seaside town are let down and count their money.
explanation.definitionFit: To budget is to plan spending against available money, weighing up resources.

clue.text: Inflicted criticism on horse: 'Good finisher, lacking heart'

indicators.note: without its heart, the middle letter goes

explanation.surface: A racing tipster harshly judges a horse as a strong closer with no courage.
explanation.definitionFit: To nag someone is to pester them with persistent complaints and faultfinding.
